sentences.text: The fossil material consists of the rear part of a skull, isolated teeth, the first neck vertebra, and two armor plates.
The genus name merges the Japanese term for Japan with the Greek word for shield.
The species epithet honors Yezo, the historic name for Hokkaido, where the specimen was found.
Eijiro Goto uncovered the holotype on 25 June 1995 in Yūbari, Hokkaido, Japan.
The specimen was encased in a calcareous concretion that had eroded from the Hikagenosawa Formation.
After excavation it was donated to the Mikasa City Museum and catalogued as specimen MCM A522.
Shumpei Oyabu and colleagues formally described the new genus and species in 2026, designating MCM A522 as the holotype.
Researchers infer that Nipponopelta probably lived near marine settings such as coastal and estuarine zones.
They also note that nodosaurid remains in marine deposits may reflect post-mortem transport of carcasses rather than true habitat preference.
Nipponopelta belongs to the nodosaurid family Nodosauridae.
Phylogenetic analysis places it within the Nodosaurinae subfamily, nearer to Nodosaurus and Panoplosaurus than to Polacanthus or Struthiosaurus.
It lived in the Late Cretaceous, specifically during the Cenomanian age.
Its age is estimated between 100.5 and 93.9 million years ago.
Fossils come from the Upper Cretaceous Hikagenosawa Formation of the Yezo Group in Japan.
There is ongoing debate about whether nodosaurid fossils in marine sediments indicate the animals’ actual habitats or are the result of transport after death.
